result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.edge_subgraph()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Extract a subgraph containing the specified edges and their endpoint nodes. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L22654-L22768){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.edge_subgraph(edges) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Edge-induced subgraph](/assets/graphs/edge-subgraph.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="The same six-node graph with its edges numbered 1 to 7; edges 1, 4 and 5 are requested. The result keeps exactly those three accent edges and their endpoints A, B, D, E. Edge 3 between A and D is dropped even though both endpoints stay, which is what separates this from an induced subgraph." width="100%"} Returns a new graph containing only the specified edges and the nodes that are endpoints of those edges. This is useful when you want to focus on specific relationships rather than specific nodes. Unlike `subgraph()`, which keeps every edge among the chosen nodes, this keeps only the edges you list. Two kept nodes can therefore lose an edge between them if that edge was not requested, and nodes that touch none of the listed edges are left out entirely. Common reasons to use it: - isolating one type of relationship, such as only inhibitory interactions in a signaling network - keeping the edges that pass a weight or confidence threshold, along with just the nodes they connect - extracting a path, tree, or matching found by another algorithm as its own graph The original graph is not modified. Node IDs in the new graph are renumbered, and the selection state is not carried over. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [edges]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [list[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : List of edge IDs to include in the subgraph, as found in the `id` column of `get_edge_df()` or returned by `get_edge_ids()`. Order does not matter, and repeated IDs are included once. An empty list gives an empty graph. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : New graph containing only the specified edges and their endpoint nodes. Preserves directedness, weightedness, node labels and attributes, and edge weights and attributes. Node IDs are renumbered from 1 in ascending order of the original IDs. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If any edge ID is not found in the graph. ::: ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~subgraph`) : Extract the induced subgraph on a set of nodes. [](`~transform_to_subgraph_ws`) : Extract the subgraph defined by the current selection. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Taking two of the five edges of a cycle keeps their three endpoints (the two edges share a node) and drops the rest: ::: {#651adfe8 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec # Create a cycle: 1 -- 2 -- 3 -- 4 -- 5 -- 1 graph = ec.Graph().add_cycle_graph(5) # Get first two edge IDs edge_ids = list(graph.get_edge_ids())[:2] sub = graph.edge_subgraph(edge_ids) # Returns 3 (endpoints of 2 edges) sub.count_nodes() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 3 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#b2101ee9 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Returns 2 sub.count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 2 ``` ::: ::: In K4 the first two edges both start at node `1` (`1--2` and `1--3`), so the result is a small star with three nodes and two edges: ::: {#569a94ed .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ec.Graph().add_full_graph(4) # K4 with 6 edges edge_ids = list(graph.get_edge_ids())[:2] star = graph.edge_subgraph(edge_ids) star.get_edges_str_repr(use_labels=True) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` ['1--2', '1--3'] ``` ::: ::: Filtering on an edge attribute pulls out one kind of relationship. Only the two `"inhibits"` edges survive; nodes `A` and `B` are both kept, yet their `"activates"` edge is gone, which an induced subgraph would have kept: ::: {#99473401 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} g = ec.Graph(directed=True) g.add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D"]) g.add_edges( [ ("A", "B", {"rel": "activates"}), ("B", "C", {"rel": "inhibits"}), ("C", "D", {"rel": "activates"}), ("A", "D", {"rel": "inhibits"}), ] ) edf = g.get_edge_df() inhibitory = edf.filter(edf["rel"] == "inhibits")["id"].to_list() g.edge_subgraph(inhibitory).get_edges_str_repr(use_labels=True) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` ['B->C', 'A->D'] ``` ::: :::
